adana.name: Adana
adana.summary: A large city in southern Turkey on the Seyhan River, at the heart of the Cilicia region, historically important for its mountain pass, trade routes, and metal and agricultural wealth.

kizzuwatna.name: Kizzuwatna
kizzuwatna.summary: An ancient Anatolian kingdom attested from the late 16th century BC, located in the Cilician Plain of southeastern Anatolia with its center at Kummanni.

alaca-h-y-k.name: Alaca Höyük
alaca-h-y-k.summary: A Neolithic and Hittite archaeological site in central Turkey, near the ancient Hittite capital Hattusa.

royal-cemetery-at-ur.name: Royal Cemetery at Ur
royal-cemetery-at-ur.summary: An archaeological site in southern Iraq excavated between 1922 and 1934 by Leonard Woolley for the British Museum and University of Pennsylvania, its finds now held mainly in Baghdad and London.

kura-araxes-culture.name: Kura–Araxes culture
kura-araxes-culture.summary: Archaeological culture that existed from about 4000 to 2000 BC across the Caucasus and nearby regions, marked by a sedentary agricultural economy and named after the Kura and Araxes river valleys.

karum-trade-post.name: Karum
karum-trade-post.summary: Ancient Old Assyrian trade posts in Anatolia active from the 20th to 18th centuries BC, with their main center at the town of Kanesh.

k-ltepe.name: Kültepe (Kanesh)
k-ltepe.summary: Archaeological site in Turkey, also known as Kanesh or Neša, a major Bronze Age settlement whose lower city held an Assyrian trading district and yielded over 23,500 cuneiform tablets.

alazani.name: Alazani
alazani.summary: 351-kilometre river in the Caucasus and main tributary of the Kura, forming part of the border between Georgia and Azerbaijan, likely the river ancient authors called Alazonius.

hittite-wars-of-survival.name: Hittite Wars of Survival
hittite-wars-of-survival.summary: A series of wars (c. 1400–1350 BC) between the Hittite Empire and neighbors such as Arzawa, Kaška and Hayasa-Azzi, in which the Hittite capital Ḫattuša was sacked before King Šuppiluliuma regained all the lost territory.

arzawa.name: Arzawa
arzawa.summary: A Bronze Age kingdom and confederation of states in western Anatolia with shifting ties to the Hittites, briefly recognized by Egypt as an independent power before being conquered around 1300 BC.

kaskians.name: Kaska
kaskians.summary: A Bronze Age non-Indo-European people living in the mountainous Black Sea region of Anatolia, known from Hittite sources, whose presence blocked Hittite expansion northward.

hattusa.name: Hattusa
hattusa.summary: Capital of the Hittite Empire in the late Bronze Age, in modern Turkey; its ruins were rediscovered in 1834 and named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

uppiluliuma-i.name: Šuppiluliuma I
uppiluliuma-i.summary: A Hittite king who reigned from about 1350 to 1322 BC, expanding Hittite power over Mittani and northern Syria; a failed marriage proposal to Egypt's widowed queen brought long hostility between the two empires.

late-bronze-age-collapse.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
late-bronze-age-collapse.summary: A sudden societal collapse across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, ending major Bronze Age powers like the Hittite Empire.

arnuwanda-i.name: Arnuwanda I
arnuwanda-i.summary: Hittite great king who ruled in the early 14th century BC, around 1390 to 1380/1370 BC.

ma-at-h-y-k.name: Maşat Höyük
ma-at-h-y-k.summary: A Bronze Age Hittite archaeological site in north-central Turkey, believed to be the ancient city of Tapikka, first excavated in the 1970s.

ku-akl-sarissa.name: Sarissa (Kuşaklı)
ku-akl-sarissa.summary: An archaeological site in Turkey known in Hittite times as Sarissa, located near modern Sivas.

tud-aliya-i.name: Tudḫaliya I/II
tud-aliya-i.summary: Hittite great king who ruled around 1465 to 1440 BC, sometimes considered identical with the later Tudḫaliya II.

assuwa.name: Assuwa
assuwa.summary: A confederation of 22 states in western Anatolia around 1400 BC that formed to oppose the Hittite Empire and was defeated under Tudhaliya I/II.

tar-unna.name: Tarḫunna
tar-unna.summary: The Hittite weather god, also known as the Weather God of Heaven or the Lord of the Land of Hatti.

tud-aliya-iii.name: Tudḫaliya III
tud-aliya-iii.summary: Hittite great king who ruled Anatolia around 1380 to 1350 BC, father of Šuppiluliuma I; later texts portray his reign as a time when the kingdom neared collapse.

lola-culture.name: Lola culture
lola-culture.summary: A Middle Bronze Age culture that flourished in the North Caucasus and Volga-Ural steppes from about 2200 to 1800 BC.

srubnaya-culture.name: Srubnaya culture
srubnaya-culture.summary: An Iranic Late Bronze Age culture (1900–1200 BCE) in the eastern Pontic-Caspian steppe, successor to the Yamnaya culture and generally linked to early Iranian speakers.

madduwatta.name: Madduwatta
madduwatta.summary: Late Bronze Age warlord who conquered part of southwest Anatolia, known from the Hittite text called the Indictment of Madduwatta.

mycenaean-greece.name: Mycenaean Greece
mycenaean-greece.summary: A late Bronze Age Greek civilization, lasting roughly 1750 to 1050 BC, marked by palatial states, art, and the Linear B writing system.

achaeans-homer.name: Ahhiyawa
achaeans-homer.summary: A term in Hittite and Egyptian Late Bronze Age texts believed to refer to the Mycenaean civilization, linguistically related to Homer's name "Achaeans" for the Greeks.

hayasa-azzi.name: Hayasa-Azzi
hayasa-azzi.summary: A Late Bronze Age confederation in the Armenian Highlands or Pontic region that fought the Hittite Empire in the 14th century BC and is thought to have shaped the ethnogenesis of Armenians.

alaksandu.name: Alaksandu
alaksandu.summary: King of Wilusa around 1280 BCE who sealed a treaty with the Hittite king Muwatalli II; his name may be linked to the Greek name Alexander.

wilusa.name: Wilusa
wilusa.summary: Late Bronze Age city in western Anatolia known from Hittite records, notable for its identification with the site of Troy and the legendary Trojan War.

muwatalli-ii.name: Muwatalli II
muwatalli-ii.summary: King of the Hittite New Kingdom empire, ruling roughly from 1295 to 1272 BC (short chronology).

apaliunas.name: Apaliunas
apaliunas.summary: A protective deity of the city of Wilusa named in a Hittite treaty around 1280 BCE, thought to be an early form of the god Apollo.

isuwa.name: Ishuwa
isuwa.summary: An ancient kingdom founded by the Hurrians that came under Hittite control around 1600 BC after conflict with the Hittites.

attarsiya.name: Attarsiya
attarsiya.summary: Mycenaean Greek warlord active around 1400 BC, known from a single Hittite text describing his campaigns in western Anatolia, the earliest record of Mycenaean involvement there.

battle-of-kadesh.name: Battle of Kadesh
battle-of-kadesh.summary: A major c.1274 BCE battle between Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittites, the earliest pitched battle in recorded history with known tactics, ending in stalemate.

walmu.name: Walmu
walmu.summary: A king of Wiluša (likely the site of Troy) in the late 13th century BC, known only from a single surviving letter describing his overthrow and the Hittites' plan to restore him to his throne.

milawata-letter.name: Milawata letter
milawata-letter.summary: A diplomatic letter from a Hittite king to a client king in western Anatolia around 1240 BC, demanding resolution of a hostage dispute and reinstatement of a deposed ruler, and an important source on the historicity of Homer's Iliad.

mur-ili-ii.name: Mursili II
mur-ili-ii.summary: King of the Hittite Empire, reigning around 1330 to 1295 BC (or 1321–1295 BC by another chronology).

seha-river-land.name: Seha River Land
seha-river-land.summary: A Late Bronze Age kingdom in Western Anatolia, part of Arzawa, located between Mira and Wilusa and at times controlling the island of Lazpa.

manapa-tarhunta.name: Manapa-Tarhunta
manapa-tarhunta.summary: King of the Seha River Land in western Anatolia during the Late Bronze Age, born around the 1330s BC as a younger son of King Muwa-Walwis, known from Hittite royal archives.

miletus.name: Miletus
miletus.summary: Ancient Greek city on Anatolia's western coast, a wealthy maritime and trading power that founded dozens of Mediterranean and Black Sea colonies and was home to early philosophers such as Thales; known in Hittite records as Millawata.

tarkasnawa.name: Tarkasnawa
tarkasnawa.summary: Bronze Age ruler of the kingdom of Mira in western Anatolia and one of the last independent kings of the Arzawa confederation, known from inscriptions and royal seals.

mira-kingdom.name: Mira
mira-kingdom.summary: A Late Bronze Age vassal kingdom (c. 1330–1190 BC) in western Anatolia that emerged after the Hittites broke up the larger kingdom of Arzawa.

tud-aliya-iv.name: Tudḫaliya IV
tud-aliya-iv.summary: King of the Hittite Empire who reigned around 1245 to 1215 BC, son of Ḫattušili III and Queen Puduḫepa.

sintashta-culture.name: Sintashta culture
sintashta-culture.summary: A Middle Bronze Age archaeological culture of the Southern Urals (c. 2200–1900 BCE), thought to be the origin of the Indo-Iranian languages and the earliest known chariots, with fortified, militaristic settlements.

andronovo-culture.name: Andronovo culture
andronovo-culture.summary: A group of related Late Bronze Age cultures from about 2000 to 1150 BCE, spanning from the southern Urals to central Siberia and western Xinjiang, generally agreed to have been Indo-Iranian.

kaman-kaleh-y-k.name: Kaman-Kalehöyük
kaman-kaleh-y-k.summary: A multi-period archaeological mound in central Turkey, about 100 km from Ankara and from the Hittite capital Hattusa, occupied from the Bronze Age through Ottoman times.

neo-hittite-states.name: Neo-Hittite states
neo-hittite-states.summary: Luwian and Aramean regional states in Iron Age Turkey and Syria that arose after the Hittite New Kingdom's collapse in the 12th century BCE and lasted until Assyria conquered them in the 8th century BCE.

sea-peoples.name: Sea Peoples
sea-peoples.summary: A group of tribes who raided Egypt and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, once seen as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse but now often viewed as refugees fleeing an ongoing crisis.

hittites.name: Hittites
hittites.summary: An Anatolian Indo-European people who built one of the first major Bronze Age civilizations in West Asia, forming an empire centered on the capital Hattusa that peaked in the mid-14th century BC under Šuppiluliuma I before collapsing by the 12th century BC.

middle-assyrian-empire.name: Middle Assyrian Empire
middle-assyrian-empire.summary: Assyria's first period as an empire, from about 1363 BC to 912 BC, during which it became the dominant power of northern Mesopotamia.

mitanni.name: Mitanni
mitanni.summary: A Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia, around 1550 to 1260 BCE, a major regional power bordered by the Hittites, Egyptians, Kassites and Assyrians.

anitta-text.name: Anitta
anitta-text.summary: Bronze Age king of Kussara around 1700 BCE, recorded in the oldest known text in an Indo-European language; he defeated the king of Zalpuwa and the Hattic king Piyusti, then destroyed and cursed Piyusti's capital, the site that later became the Hittite capital of Hattusa.

kussara.name: Kussara
kussara.summary: A Middle Bronze Age kingdom in Anatolia, remembered mainly as the origin of the dynasty that founded the Old Hittite Kingdom.

piyusti.name: Piyushti
piyusti.summary: An 18th/17th-century BC king of Hattusa, defeated at least twice by King Anitta according to the Anitta text.

new-kingdom-of-egypt.name: New Kingdom of Egypt
new-kingdom-of-egypt.summary: The period of ancient Egypt from about the 16th to 11th century BC, covering the 18th to 20th dynasties, marking Egypt's greatest power and territorial extent.

attu-ili-i.name: Ḫattušili I
attu-ili-i.summary: A king of the Hittite Old Kingdom who reigned roughly from 1650 to 1620 BC and died around 1620 BC.

tukulti-ninurta-i.name: Tukulti-Ninurta I
tukulti-ninurta-i.summary: King of Assyria who reigned around 1243 to 1207 BC and was the first ruler known to use the title 'King of Kings.'

mysians.name: Mysians
mysians.summary: The ancient inhabitants of Mysia, a region in northwestern Asia Minor.

uppiluliuma-ii.name: Šuppiluliuma II
uppiluliuma-ii.summary: Last known great king of the Hittite New Kingdom, reigning about 1207 to 1178 BC; his fleet defeated the Cypriots in what is recorded as history's first naval battle.

kummanni.name: Kummanni
kummanni.summary: Main center of the Anatolian kingdom of Kizzuwatna and major cult site of the Hurrian chief god Tešup, whose exact location is uncertain but was likely in Cilicia.

lawazantiya.name: Lawazantiya
lawazantiya.summary: A major Bronze Age city in the Kingdom of Kizzuwatna, sacred to the goddess Šauška and known for a temple fed by seven springs.

cilicia.name: Cilicia
cilicia.summary: A geographical region of southern Anatolia along the Mediterranean coast, historically bordering Pamphylia, Cappadocia and Syria, now covering Turkey's Mersin, Adana, Osmaniye and Hatay provinces.

pudu-epa.name: Puduhepa
pudu-epa.summary: A Hittite queen of the 13th century BC, married to King Hattusili III and described as one of the most influential women known from the ancient Near East.

attu-ili-iii.name: Ḫattušili III
attu-ili-iii.summary: King of the Hittite New Kingdom empire around 1275 to 1245 BC.

epat.name: Ḫepat
epat.summary: A goddess linked to the city of Aleppo from the third millennium BCE, worshipped across the region as the spouse of storm gods, including Teshub in Hurrian religion.

luwian-language.name: Luwian language
luwian-language.summary: An ancient Indo-European language, or group of languages, of Anatolia, written in cuneiform or hieroglyphic scripts and named after the region of Luwiya.

kamru-epa.name: Kamrušepa
kamru-epa.summary: A Hittite and Luwian goddess of medicine and magic, best known for her role in the Telepinu Myth in pacifying an angry vegetation god.

hattians.name: Hattians
hattians.summary: An ancient Bronze Age people of central Anatolia speaking a language unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European tongues, gradually absorbed by the Hittites by about 1700 BC.

luwians.name: Luwians
luwians.summary: An ancient Anatolian people who spoke the Luwian language, part of the Hittite Empire in the Bronze Age and later founders of Neo-Hittite states in northern Syria.

luwian-religion.name: Luwian religion
luwian-religion.summary: The religious beliefs and practices of the Luwians of Anatolia, traceable from the Bronze Age to the early Roman Empire and shaped by neighboring Syrian and Hurrian influences.

hurrian-religion.name: Hurrian Religion
hurrian-religion.summary: The polytheistic religion of the Hurrians, a Bronze Age Near Eastern people, blending native deities with Mesopotamian, Syrian, Anatolian and Elamite influences and shaping Hittite religion.

tar-unz.name: Tarḫunz
tar-unz.summary: The chief weather god of the Luwians, a Bronze and early Iron Age Anatolian people, closely related to the Hittite god Tarḫunna.

arma-deity.name: Arma
arma-deity.summary: Anatolian Moon god worshipped by the Hittites and Luwians during the Bronze Age and early Iron Age.

runtiya.name: Runtiya
runtiya.summary: The Luwian god of the hunt, closely associated with deer and among the most important deities of the Luwians.

palaic-language.name: Palaic
palaic-language.summary: An extinct Indo-European language recorded on Bronze Age cuneiform tablets in the Hittite capital Hattusa, likely spoken in northern Anatolia until around the 15th century BCE.

uwa-anna.name: Ḫuwaššanna
uwa-anna.summary: A goddess of Hittite and Luwian religion in the second millennium BCE, chief deity of the city of Ḫupišna, no longer worshipped after that millennium.

trialeti-vanadzor-culture.name: Trialeti-Vanadzor culture
trialeti-vanadzor-culture.summary: A Bronze Age culture named after regions in Georgia and Armenia, flourishing in the late 3rd to early 2nd millennium BCE, marked by advances in metallurgy and social stratification and possibly an early Proto-Armenian culture.

shengavit-site.name: Shengavit
shengavit-site.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site near Yerevan, Armenia, inhabited from about 3000 to 2500 BCE, and a type site for the Kura-Araxes culture.

boris-kuftin.name: Boris Kuftin
boris-kuftin.summary: A Soviet archaeologist and ethnographer (1892–1953) who discovered the Trialeti culture in the 1930s and coined the term Kura-Araxes in 1940.

tamaz-v-gamkrelidze.name: Tamaz Gamkrelidze
tamaz-v-gamkrelidze.summary: Georgian linguist, orientalist and Hittitologist (1929–2021) who led the Georgian Academy of Sciences as president from 2005 to 2013.

vyacheslav-ivanov-philologist.name: Vyacheslav Ivanov
vyacheslav-ivanov-philologist.summary: Soviet and Russian philologist and Indo-Europeanist (1929-2017), best known for the glottalic theory of Indo-European consonants and for placing the Indo-European homeland near the Armenian highlands.

lchashen-metsamor-culture.name: Lchashen–Metsamor culture
lchashen-metsamor-culture.summary: A Late Bronze and Early Iron Age archaeological culture, 1500 to 700 BCE, found mainly in present-day Armenia, with pottery also found in Turkey and Georgia.
